g00.shop-setup.why: a bench that is out of level twists the practice pieces before any glass is on them

g00.tools.why: the cloth and the tools have to be on the bench before the cup is mixed
scissors follow a marked line without pulling the weave out of square
the buddy pair holds the cloth while the owner wets it, which is how a large skin gets laid

g00.mix.why: weigh 100 parts of resin to 40 of hardener, then stir the walls and the bottom

g00.orientation.why: BID is cut on the bias and UND is cut with its warp along the load
bias BID takes shear and drapes; UND puts its strength along the warp

g00.flat-layup.why: cut all six BID plies on the bias before the cup is mixed
the first ply sets the fiber direction for the rectangle
the brush pushes resin through the weave until no white cloth remains
resin left in this ply is what pushes the cured weight over 12.5 ounces
the next ply goes down only after the one below is wet
wet this ply through before covering it
pull the spare resin out so the ply stays near the cloth weight
the third ply crosses the stack the same way
a dry spot in the middle cannot be fixed after the next ply covers it
work the spare resin to the edge, where the trim will cut it off
the fourth ply follows the same bias as the first
wet the ply out fully; a starved ply is the light, white rectangle
squeegee until the weave shows, not until the cloth goes white
the fifth ply is still bias BID, same as the rest of this rectangle
wet it before the last ply hides any dry strand
keep this ply as lean as the ones under it
the sixth ply closes the practice stack
the last ply is the one the weight check is most sensitive to
the target is about 11 ounces for the trimmed 10 by 16 inch piece
trim and weigh only after this stack has cured

g00.peel-ply.why: peel ply stays on through the cure and keeps air off the last ply
squeegee on the peel ply so the fibers under it do not drag

g00.micro-flox.why: dry micro fills the inside corner so the glass does not crease over a sharp edge
flox is the paste that carries load; micro is only the light filler

g00.foam-shape.why: the hot wire is the core-cutting tool, practiced here on scrap rather than on a flight core
urethane sands away under the block, so a ridge becomes a bump in the glass
a string shows a bow that the eye reads as straight
the beam has to sit level before it is glassed or the cure locks in a twist

g00.load-beam.why: the urethane core is on the bench before any cloth touches it
push spare resin to the edges and trim those edges after the cure
the load across the round support waits until the beam has cured

g00.bookend.why: the back face is glassed only after the front face has cured
sand the cured glass dull or the next plies will not stick
this is the last practice cure; the airplane steps wait on it

f05.side-layout.why: cut the dish and the sight-gauge groove

lay release tape over the marked areas

f05.inside-layup.why: the buddy mixes and passes resin while you wet out
the second ply crosses the first at the opposite angle
flox in the top longeron, stiffener and aft blocks

f05.spar-cutout.why: remove the foam and glass block
remove the foam and glass block
